title: Report Title
text:
About This Report
This is a report template for the Dynamic Learning Maps® (DLM®) Alternate Assessment System. This is where we can provide a brief overview or purpose of the manual. If this is a technical report, this is where we would include the executive summary.

title: Report Title
text:
Acknowledgments
Here we can include any acknowledgements (e.g., staff, advisory committees).

title: 1  Text Features
text:
1.1 Conditional text
There are several ways to include text optionally. First, we can use in-line helpers such as dlm_is_pdf() or dlm_is_html(), which can be used to determine the type of output. For example, this is the website version of this report.
We can also include or exclude entire paragraphs using the the .content-visible class with a div.
Read this report chapter by chapter in the browser, or download the complete PDF from the button above.

title: 1  Text Features
text:
1.2 Callouts
Callouts can be used to draw attention to some text. Create a callout with:
::: {.callout-note}
## Callout title

Here is the callout text.
:::

Create a tip callout using the .callout-tip class.








ImportantImportant callout



Create an important callout using the .callout-important class.








WarningWarning callout



Create a warning callout using the .callout-warning class.








CautionCaution callout



Create a caution callout using the .callout-caution class.

title: 1  Text Features
text:
1.6 Citations
We can include a normal reference (Thompson, 2026). Or we can include in text, such as with Clark (2016). We can also include an abbreviation, like for the loglinear cognitive diagnostic model (LCDM; Henson et al., 2009).

title: 1  Text Features
text:
1.7 Equations
Equations can also be rendered, numbered, and references as shown in Equation 1.1.
\[
P(X_j = x_j) = \sum_{c=1}^C\nu_c \prod_{i=1}^I\pi_{ic}^{x_{ij}}(1-\pi_{ic})^{1 - x_{ij}}
\tag{1.1}\]
We can also render math inline. For example, the intercept of Equation 1.2, \(\lambda_{i,0}\), determines the probability of a correct response for a nonmaster, and the main effect \(\lambda_{i,1}\) is the increase in log-odds associated with mastery.
\[
\pi_{ic} = P(X_{ic} = 1|\alpha_c) = \frac{\exp(\lambda_{i,0} + \lambda_{i,1}\alpha_c)}{1 + \exp(\lambda_{i,0} + \lambda_{i,1}\alpha_c)}
\tag{1.2}\]




Clark, A. K. (2016). Item writing and review practices for alternate assessments.


Henson, R. A., Templin, J. L., & Willse, J. T. (2009). Defining a family of cognitive diagnosis models using log-linear models with latent variables. Psychometrika, 74(2), 191–210. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-008-9089-5


Thompson, W. J. (2026). Measr: Bayesian psychometric measurement using stan. https://measr.info

title: 2  Figures
text:
2.1 Standard figures
This chapter focuses on figures. The Typst output format enforces A-2a and UA-1 standards, meaning that all figures are required to have alternative text specified via the fig-alt chunk option. If there are any figures without alternative text specified, the render will fail.
Figure 2.1 is a standard figure with the default figure size and aspect ratio.

We can also add facets and change the aspect ratio, as shown in Figure 2.2.

title: 2  Figures
text:
2.3 Complex figure captions
For captions that require markdown formatting, we recommend setting the figure within a div as shown below. Additionally, can provide a fig-scap, which is a shorter version of the caption. The fig-scap will be printed in the List of Figures at the beginning of the PDF document, whereas the full caption will be used in the text. When using the div approach below, the full caption is included after the R chunk that generates the figure.
::: {#fig-pct-proficient fig-scap="Percentage of students proficient by grade"}

```{r}
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Line plot showing the percentage of student proficient by grade and
#|   subject.

example_dat |>
  mutate(proficient = pl %in% c("At Target", "Advanced")) |>
  summarize(pct_proficient = mean(proficient), .by = c(grade, subject)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(grade), y = pct_proficient)) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(subject)) +
  geom_line(group = 1) +
  labs(x = "Grade", y = "% Proficient")
```

Percentage of student proficient by grade (*N* = `r fmt_count(nrow(example_dat))`)

:::














Figure 2.4: Percentage of students proficient by grade (N = 14,005)

title: 2  Figures
text:
2.4 Figure notes
Use the fig-note chunk option to add a note below a figure’s caption, as shown in Figure 2.5. The note is formatted as markdown and is left out of the List of Figures. For a figure placed in a div, fig-note can be set as an attribute on the div instead, similar to fig-scap in Section 2.3 (e.g., ::: {#fig-example fig-note="..."}).








Figure 2.5: Distribution of performance levels for grades 3–8Note. Grades with fewer than 20 students (n < 20) were omitted.

title: 3  Tables
text:
3.1 Standard tables
This chapter focuses on tables. Tables are created with the gt package, and the gt_atlas() helper defined in _common.R applies the house formatting: decimal alignment, one decimal place for counts and percentages, three decimal places with no leading zero for values bounded by −1 and 1 (e.g., correlations and proportions), and an indent for rows within row groups. Captions are placed above tables, and table numbers are added automatically from the tbl- label.

Tables can also contain longer text. Column widths can be set with cols_width() so that text wraps within cells, as in Table 3.3. Table 3.3 also includes a footnote attached to a single cell, created with tab_footnote(). Use opt_footnote_marks(marks = "standard") to use symbols (*, †, ‡) rather than numbers, which could be confused with values in the table.
